# libtmux-lisp
Capture and automate tmux workspaces in native Common Lisp. Acquire a CLOS object graph once, process its panes with ordinary sequences, and make mutations through an explicit client. **Implemented:** captured sessions, physical windows, window links and panes; bounded subprocess transport; cancellation; named operations, byte buffers, validated native queries, eager QuerySets, optional regex and bounded JSON; [bounded declarative workspaces](docs/workspaces.md) with pure plans, explicit apply and an explicit-endpoint CLI; [typed option, hook and environment mutations](docs/operations.md#configuration-mutations) for the exact reviewed tmux catalogs through 3.8; explicit entity and server termination with retained outcome evidence. **In development:** decoded configuration readers, control/events and streaming. MCP is intentionally out of scope. The `0.1.0` systems are unreleased. ## Install from source Use Linux x86-64 (including WSL), kernel 6.9+, Bash and a native tmux 3.3a+ binary. Plain tmux 3.3 is rejected. The pinned toolchain is SBCL 2.6.10, ASDF/UIOP 3.3.7 and Qlot 1.8.4, managed by [mise 2026.11.3+](https://mise.jdx.dev/getting-started.html). ASDF is the Lisp build system; asdf-vm is not required. ```console $ git clone https://github.com/libtmux/libtmux-lisp.git && cd libtmux-lisp ``` Review [mise.toml](mise.toml), then trust the checkout: ```console $ mise trust ``` ```console $ mise install ``` Install the locked dependencies. This is the network step: ```console $ mise run setup ``` Run the complete workspace example. It creates a private tmux socket, checks the results and removes its daemon; it never addresses your default server. ```console $ mise run examples ``` Success includes `EXAMPLES PASS: graph, links, native, compiled, relation, regex and JSON selection, declarative workspace, false/presence, ownership, refresh, bytes, capture, close, terminate`. Core and query loading need ASDF/UIOP only; optional regex/JSON use the locked CL-PPCRE/Jzon systems. The example runner also needs Python 3. No Java runtime is involved. ## Declare and apply a workspace The optional `libtmux/workspace` ASDF system reads a closed, bounded JSON document, plans locally, and applies only through an explicit client. The shipped [`workspace.json`](examples/workspace.json) creates two windows and three panes from argv arrays. This tested function returns both the inspectable plan and retained application evidence: ```lisp (defun apply-workspace-document (client pathname) "Plan and apply one bounded workspace document through explicit CLIENT. Return the local plan steps and retained application result as two values." (let* ((workspace (ws:read-workspace pathname)) (snapshot (tm:fetch-snapshot client)) (plan (ws:plan-workspace workspace snapshot))) (values (ws:plan-steps plan) (ws:apply-workspace client workspace)))) ``` An exact second apply returns an empty plan and no command outcomes. A conflict fails before dispatch. A partial failure retains the failed step and every core outcome; no mutation is retried or rolled back. The CLI's `validate` and `plan` modes need no daemon, while `apply` requires `--socket-path`. Read the [workspace guide](docs/workspaces.md) and [generated workspace API](docs/workspace-api.md). ## Inspect a workspace The [REPL tutorial](docs/tutorial.md) loads the example package, whose local nickname `tm` refers to `libtmux`. This complete function returns ordinary owned data after closing its client: ```lisp (defun inspect-workspace (socket-path &key (program "tmux")) "Acquire one graph from SOCKET-PATH; return owned session/window/pane data." (tm:with-client (client :program program :socket-path socket-path) (let ((snapshot (tm:fetch-snapshot client))) (loop for session across (tm:sessions snapshot) collect (list :session (tm:name session) :windows (loop for link across (tm:window-links session) for window = (tm:window link) collect (list :index (tm:index link) :name (tm:name window) :panes (map 'list #'tm:entity-data (tm:panes window))))))))) ``` [libtmux:fetch-snapshot](docs/api.md#fetch-snapshot-function) contacts tmux. Traversal and projection inside the loops are local. Returned strings and sequence containers belong to the caller. Acquisition spans an interval; it is not a transaction over a changing daemon. The [walkthrough](docs/tutorial.md#build-a-linked-workspace) also creates two sessions, splits a pane and links one physical window into both sessions: ```mermaid graph LR work[Session: work] --> a[Window link: index 0] work --> b[Window link: logs] review[Session: review] --> c[Window link: index 7] review --> d[Window link: notes] a --> editor[Physical window: editor] c --> editor editor --> p1[Pane 1] editor --> p2[Pane 2] b --> logs[Physical window: logs] d --> notes[Physical window: notes] ``` Select a **window link** when session/index context matters. Rename the physical window to affect every link. Refresh returns a new observation; earlier captures retain their values. See [identity and ownership](docs/captures.md). ## Compile a local query The tutorial's example package gives `libtmux` and `libtmux.query` the local nicknames `tm` and `q`. This checked function compiles once, filters a captured vector locally, and returns ordinary owned data: ```lisp (defparameter *wide-active-filter* (q:compile-filter :pane '(:and (:= :pane/active t) (:>= :pane/width 40)))) (defun wide-active-pane-data (snapshot) "Return owned data for captured active panes at least 40 cells wide; no I/O." (map 'vector #'tm:entity-data (q:matching *wide-active-filter* (tm:panes snapshot)))) ``` `matching` returns a fresh simple vector and preserves order and duplicates. The compiler owns mutable operands, rejects cycles and mistyped fields, and never evaluates query data. Scalar filtering performs no tmux calls. Read the [query guide](docs/queries.md) for presence, limits, inspection and strict cardinality. Relations traverse the same captured graph. This checked query follows session links to physical windows and panes, then uses the eager local QuerySet: ```lisp (defparameter *active-session-filter* (q:compile-filter :session '(:any :session/window-links (:is :link/window (:any :window/panes (:= :pane/active t)))))) (defun active-session-data (snapshot) "Return owned data for sessions with an active pane; no I/O." (map 'vector #'tm:entity-data (q:items (q:where (q:from (tm:sessions snapshot) :model :session) *active-session-filter*)))) ``` ## Add regex and a versioned filter document Optional systems keep core/query dependency-free while providing a compiled CL-PPCRE scanner and a bounded native JSON envelope. These checked definitions match the demo's `cat` panes, serialize the filter, read it with explicit regex permission, and evaluate the restored predicate against the same capture: ```lisp (defparameter *cat-command-filter* (q:compile-filter :pane '(:regex-full-match :pane/current-command (:cl-ppcre "CAT" :case-insensitive-mode t)))) (defun cat-pane-data (snapshot) "Return owned data for captured panes whose command is exactly cat; no I/O." (map 'vector #'tm:entity-data (q:matching *cat-command-filter* (tm:panes snapshot)))) ``` ```lisp (defun round-trip-filter-document (snapshot) "Round-trip the checked regex filter and apply it to one retained snapshot." (let* ((document (j:write-filter *cat-command-filter*)) (restored (j:read-filter document :allow-regex t))) (values document (map 'vector #'tm:entity-data (q:matching restored (tm:panes snapshot)))))) ``` The JSON decoder rejects duplicates, unknown names, null operands and exhausted input/depth/node/string/membership/numeric bounds. It never interns external names. See [optional query interchange](docs/query-interchange.md). ## Find the right guide | Task | Start here | | --- | --- | | Load the library; inspect and build a workspace | [REPL tutorial](docs/tutorial.md) | | Filter with `loop`, handle false/absence, export plists | [Local data recipes](docs/tutorial.md#select-and-project-locally) | | Compile typed filters, traverse relations and compose QuerySets | [Native queries](docs/queries.md) · [Query API](docs/query-api.md) | | Add CL-PPCRE or exchange bounded filter documents | [Query interchange](docs/query-interchange.md) · [JSON API](docs/json-api.md) | | Validate, plan or explicitly apply a declarative workspace | [Workspaces](docs/workspaces.md) · [Workspace API](docs/workspace-api.md) | | Rename, resize, move, send input, capture, use buffers or terminate explicit targets | [Operation contracts](docs/operations.md) | | Look up signatures, multiple values and conditions | [Public API](docs/api.md) · [Captured fields](docs/fields.md) | | Understand deadlines, cancellation and cleanup | [Transport](docs/transport.md) | | Evaluate async, streaming and performance support | [Capabilities and limits](docs/capabilities.md) | | Rerun FiveAM tests at the REPL or inspect CI coverage | [Testing](docs/testing.md) · [Verification](verification.md) | | Navigate all documentation | [Guide index](docs/index.md) | Public calls block. Each client accepts one external operation at a time; concurrent reuse signals `client-busy`. Internal nonblocking pipe service does not provide an asynchronous application API. Closing a client releases its resources and leaves tmux running. [`kill-server`](docs/api.md#kill-server-function) is a separate explicit operation that proves the daemon accepted during its preflight exited. Daemon bootstrap currently requires tmux itself; the tutorial supplies the complete setup and cleanup. Named mutations preserve dispatch evidence and separate successful changes from follow-up observation failures. Inspect [command-outcome](docs/api.md#command-outcome-type) or the condition's [error-outcome](docs/api.md#error-outcome-function); never retry an uncertain mutation blindly. See [outcome handling](docs/tutorial.md#handle-command-and-observation-outcomes). The examples are shipped source, executed on isolated servers and checked for excerpt drift. CI runs exact tmux 3.3a and 3.8 on every push; the full twelve version matrix is a separate gate. No benchmark result is claimed. For changes, read [Contributing](.github/CONTRIBUTING.md) and [Writing](.github/WRITING.md). Licensed under [MIT](LICENSE). [Branding assets](docs/branding.md) include the logo, icons, and social cards.

# Capture, inspect and build a workspace

This tutorial uses an isolated existing tmux daemon. It creates two sessions,
three physical windows, four links and four panes, then inspects them through
ordinary Common Lisp data. It modifies only the daemon you start below.
Complete the [source installation](../README.md#install-from-source) first.

## Run the checked walkthrough

```console
$ mise run examples
```

The runner creates a mode-0700 temporary directory and explicit socket, clears
inherited tmux variables, starts an empty-configuration daemon, runs the shipped
Lisp examples, checks their results and terminates its own server. Assertions
check object/link counts, false with presence, identity, ownership, literal
names, refresh, byte buffers, optional regex/JSON queries and local access after
client closure. A failure exits nonzero. It leaves the optional thread library
unloaded.

Select another native tmux binary explicitly:

```console
$ LIBTMUX_TEST_TMUX=/usr/bin/tmux mise run examples
```

## Work at the REPL

For an interactive session, create a private daemon in a shell and keep that
shell open. This command prints its socket path; use that path when prompted
in Lisp. The automated runner and final cleanup helper need Python 3; the
library itself does not.

```console
$ export LIBTMUX_DEMO_DIR="$(mktemp -d /tmp/libtmux-lisp-demo-XXXXXXXX)" && \
  env -u TMUX \
    -u TMUX_PANE \
    tmux \
      -S "$LIBTMUX_DEMO_DIR/tmux.sock" \
      -f /dev/null \
      new-session \
        -d \
        -s work \
        -n editor \
        -x 120 \
        -y 40 \
        -- /bin/cat && \
  env -u TMUX \
    -u TMUX_PANE \
    tmux \
      -S "$LIBTMUX_DEMO_DIR/tmux.sock" \
      display-message \
        -p '#{pid}' \
        > "$LIBTMUX_DEMO_DIR/server-witness.txt" && \
  stat \
    -Lc '%d %i' \
    "$LIBTMUX_DEMO_DIR/tmux.sock" \
    >> "$LIBTMUX_DEMO_DIR/server-witness.txt" && \
  printf '%s\n' "$LIBTMUX_DEMO_DIR/tmux.sock"
```

Use the same terminal to start the pinned REPL:

```console
$ mise run repl
```

Load the query system, which depends on the core. The development REPL
registers the ASDF definition but does not implicitly load either system:

```lisp
(asdf:load-system "libtmux/query")
```

Load the three optional systems used later in the checked walkthrough:

```lisp
(asdf:load-system "libtmux/regex")
```

```lisp
(asdf:load-system "libtmux/json")
```

```lisp
(asdf:load-system "libtmux/workspace")
```

Load the recipe functions. Their package declares the SBCL package-local
nicknames `tm`, `q`, `j` and `ws` for the core, query, JSON and workspace
packages; the library claims no global short nicknames.

```lisp
(load "examples/workspace.lisp")
```

```lisp
(in-package #:libtmux.examples)
```

Supply the printed socket path as data, without invoking the Lisp reader:

```lisp
(defparameter *socket-path* (progn (write-line "Paste the demo socket path:")
                                 (read-line)))
```

This acquires the graph and returns one session record named `work`, containing
its `editor` window and one pane. Pane projections include identity, captured
fields, provenance and relationship IDs:

```lisp
(inspect-workspace *socket-path*)
```

## Build a linked workspace

The complete recipe is copied from [workspace.lisp](../examples/workspace.lisp).
It creates a `logs` window and `review` session, splits `editor`, shares that
physical window through index 7 of `review`, and renames logs literally.
Run it once on the fresh demo; a repeated invocation encounters existing names.

<!-- example:workspace -->
```lisp
(defun create-workspace (client)
  "Extend the demo's WORK session; return a fresh captured graph.
Creates a logs window, a second editor pane, a review session and a shared link.
The caller owns the isolated daemon; repeating this recipe there is an error."
  (let* ((before (tm:fetch-snapshot client))
         (work (find "work" (tm:sessions before) :key #'tm:name :test #'string=)))
    (unless work (error "Start the demo's WORK session first"))
    (let* ((editor-link (aref (tm:window-links work) 0))
           (editor (tm:window editor-link))
           (pane (aref (tm:panes editor) 0))
           (logs (observed-value
                  (tm:new-window client work :name "logs" :command '("/bin/cat"))))
           (review (observed-value
                    (tm:new-session client :name "review" :window-name "notes"
                                          :command '("/bin/cat")))))
      (tm:split-pane client pane :direction :horizontal :command '("/bin/cat"))
      (tm:link-window client editor-link review 7)
      (tm:rename-window client logs "logs #{literal}")
      (tm:fetch-snapshot client))))
```
<!-- /example -->

Keep a captured graph after closing the client. These globals are interactive
scratch values, not a global connection convention in the library:

```lisp
(defparameter *snapshot*
  (tm:with-client (client :socket-path *socket-path*)
    (create-workspace client)))
```

```lisp
(list (length (tm:sessions *snapshot*))
      (length (tm:windows *snapshot*))
      (length (tm:window-links *snapshot*))
      (length (tm:panes *snapshot*)))
```

The result is `(2 3 4 4)`. The two editor links have different session/index
locators and the same physical window. `windows` on a snapshot deduplicates
physical windows; `windows` on a session retains one entry per link.
The [graph contract](captures.md) explains all traversal directions.

## Select and project locally

<!-- example:selection -->
```lisp
(defun wide-active-panes (snapshot)
  "Select captured active panes at least 40 cells wide; no tmux commands."
  (loop for pane across (tm:panes snapshot)
        when (and (tm:active-p pane) (>= (tm:width pane) 40))
          collect (tm:entity-data pane)))
```
<!-- /example -->

```lisp
(wide-active-panes *snapshot*)
```

This returns a nonempty list of plists from the retained graph. You can instead
use `map`, `find-if`, `count-if`, `reduce` or `remove-if` with a native function.
These calls do not acquire state.

Compile a reusable scalar filter when the selection should be validated,
inspected or shared. The example package's local nickname `q` refers to
`libtmux.query`; the library claims no global nickname.

<!-- example:query -->
```lisp
(defparameter *wide-active-filter*
  (q:compile-filter
   :pane
   '(:and (:= :pane/active t)
          (:>= :pane/width 40))))

(defun wide-active-pane-data (snapshot)
  "Return owned data for captured active panes at least 40 cells wide; no I/O."
  (map 'vector #'tm:entity-data
       (q:matching *wide-active-filter* (tm:panes snapshot))))
```
<!-- /example -->

```lisp
(wide-active-pane-data *snapshot*)
```

`matching` returns a fresh simple vector in captured order. Compilation copies
the query form and checks field types, cycles and resource limits. The returned
predicate is ordinary Lisp code over retained observations; neither compilation
nor matching contacts tmux.

Traverse registered relationships without reacquiring state, and keep the eager
selection in a QuerySet with explicit root-model metadata:

<!-- example:relation -->
```lisp
(defparameter *active-session-filter*
  (q:compile-filter
   :session
   '(:any :session/window-links
     (:is :link/window
      (:any :window/panes
       (:= :pane/active t))))))

(defun active-session-data (snapshot)
  "Return owned data for sessions with an active pane; no I/O."
  (map 'vector #'tm:entity-data
       (q:items
        (q:where (q:from (tm:sessions snapshot) :model :session)
                 *active-session-filter*))))
```
<!-- /example -->

See the [native query guide](queries.md) for quantifier identities, stable
ordering, ownership and strict cardinality.

## Match and serialize an optional query

`libtmux/regex` adds CL-PPCRE-backed operators without adding that dependency
to core or `libtmux/query`. The scanner is compiled once with the filter; this
full-match example also proves that a match beginning at position zero works:

<!-- example:regex -->
```lisp
(defparameter *cat-command-filter*
  (q:compile-filter
   :pane
   '(:regex-full-match :pane/current-command
     (:cl-ppcre "CAT" :case-insensitive-mode t))))

(defun cat-pane-data (snapshot)
  "Return owned data for captured panes whose command is exactly cat; no I/O."
  (map 'vector #'tm:entity-data
       (q:matching *cat-command-filter* (tm:panes snapshot))))
```
<!-- /example -->

```lisp
(cat-pane-data *snapshot*)
```

`libtmux/json` writes the native schema `libtmux.lisp.filter/1`. Reading regex
is an explicit local opt-in because parser limits do not interrupt CL-PPCRE
scanner execution:

<!-- example:filterdocument -->
```lisp
(defun round-trip-filter-document (snapshot)
  "Round-trip the checked regex filter and apply it to one retained snapshot."
  (let* ((document (j:write-filter *cat-command-filter*))
         (restored (j:read-filter document :allow-regex t)))
    (values document
            (map 'vector #'tm:entity-data
                 (q:matching restored (tm:panes snapshot))))))
```
<!-- /example -->

```lisp
(round-trip-filter-document *snapshot*)
```

Both operations are local. The [interchange guide](query-interchange.md)
documents the closed envelope, limits and false/empty/null distinctions.

Use both values when false and absence matter. This field is always present;
an inactive pane returns `nil` and `t`:

```lisp
(let ((pane (find-if-not #'tm:active-p (tm:panes *snapshot*))))
  (multiple-value-bind (value present-p) (tm:field-value pane :pane/active)
    (list value present-p)))
```

Returned strings, plists and relation vectors are caller-owned copies.
`entity-data` is finite and contains relationship identifiers rather than a
recursive graph. A copied plist is local data; editing it does not mutate tmux.
See the [field reference](fields.md) for types and optional values.

## Handle command and observation outcomes

Creation and named mutations return
[command-outcome](api.md#command-outcome-type). A successful command
can have no replacement observation because the target disappeared afterward.
Check the observation separately; this helper never retries the mutation:

<!-- example:outcome -->
```lisp
(defun observed-value (outcome)
  "Return an operation's observed value, or signal its observation failure."
  (when (tm:outcome-observation-error outcome)
    (error (tm:outcome-observation-error outcome)))
  (multiple-value-bind (value present-p) (tm:outcome-value outcome)
    (unless present-p
      (error "This operation did not return an observation"))
    value))
```
<!-- /example -->

Rename a captured physical window and inspect old and new observations:

```lisp
(tm:with-client (client :socket-path *socket-path*)
  (let* ((snapshot (tm:fetch-snapshot client))
         (window (find "editor" (tm:windows snapshot) :key #'tm:name :test #'string=))
         (renamed (observed-value (tm:rename-window client window "api #{literal}"))))
    (list (tm:name window) (tm:name renamed) (tm:same-entity-p window renamed))))
```

The result is `("editor" "api #{literal}" t)`. The literal format punctuation
survives. Refresh uses the **same client context** and returns another captured
observation. Observations from a different connection are not interchangeable
operational targets, even when their numeric IDs match.

External failures signal typed conditions. A handler can inspect
[error-outcome](api.md#error-outcome-function),
[outcome-status](api.md#outcome-status-function),
[outcome-phase](api.md#outcome-phase-function),
[outcome-exit-code](api.md#outcome-exit-code-function) and owned
diagnostic bytes. Missing completion evidence can mean the mutation already
happened; an automatic retry can duplicate effects. The
[operation guide](operations.md#outcomes-and-target-checks) defines these cases.

## Preserve binary data

<!-- example:buffers -->
```lisp
(defun round-trip-bytes (client)
  "Store and retrieve a named binary buffer, including NUL and invalid UTF-8."
  (let ((bytes (make-array 5 :element-type '(unsigned-byte 8)
                           :initial-contents '(0 10 92 195 255))))
    (tm:set-buffer client bytes :name "example bytes")
    (multiple-value-bind (actual outcome)
        (tm:show-buffer client :name "example bytes")
      (assert (eq :succeeded (tm:outcome-status outcome)))
      (assert (equalp bytes actual))
      actual)))
```
<!-- /example -->

```lisp
(tm:with-client (client :socket-path *socket-path*) (round-trip-bytes client))
```

This returns five octets, including NUL and invalid UTF-8, unchanged. For pane
contents, `capture-pane` returns UTF-8 text and outcome; use
`capture-pane-bytes` for octets. Captures and buffer reads are bounded complete
results, not subscriptions or streams.

Successful input dispatch does not prove application readiness or consumption.
Coordinate with an application signal; do not add a sleep or treat printed
text as proof. `pipe-pane` configures a daemon-owned shell pipe and has a
separate [ownership contract](operations.md#pane-processes).

## Drive an application without polling

The shipped [worker](../examples/worker.sh) signals initialization, reads one
request, writes its receipt file, then signals consumption. The Lisp controller
uses a fresh `wait-for` channel for each signal. The file receipt proves what
the application consumed; a successful send or printed marker would not.
These are blocking calls with deadlines, not a control-mode subscription API.

<!-- example:worker -->
```lisp
(defun drive-worker (client session socket-path program worker-path receipt-path)
  "Launch a worker through argv, wait for readiness and verify input consumption.
WORKER-PATH names the shipped worker.sh; RECEIPT-PATH is in the owned demo directory.
Signals operational conditions without retrying a mutation. Calls block."
  (let* ((ready (symbol-name (gensym "example-ready-")))
         (consumed (symbol-name (gensym "example-consumed-")))
         (window (observed-value
                  (tm:new-window client session :name "worker"
                                 :command (list "/bin/sh" worker-path program
                                                socket-path ready consumed receipt-path))))
         (pane (aref (tm:panes window) 0))
         (message "release #{literal}; λ"))
    (tm:run-command client (list "-N" "wait-for" ready)
                    :effect :read :timeout 1 :output-limit 4096)
    (tm:send-text client pane message :enter t)
    (tm:run-command client (list "-N" "wait-for" consumed)
                    :effect :read :timeout 1 :output-limit 4096)
    (let ((receipt (uiop:read-file-string receipt-path :external-format :utf-8)))
      (assert (string= message receipt))
      (list :consumed receipt :pane (tm:id pane)))))
```
<!-- /example -->

```lisp
(tm:with-client (client :socket-path *socket-path*)
  (let ((session (find "work" (tm:fetch-sessions client) :key #'tm:name :test #'string=)))
    (drive-worker client session *socket-path* "tmux"
                  (namestring (truename "examples/worker.sh"))
                  (namestring (merge-pathnames "worker-receipt.txt"
                               (uiop:pathname-directory-pathname *socket-path*))))))
```

The result contains `:consumed "release #{literal}; λ"` and a pane ID. The
request travels as literal text; worker arguments travel through argv. The
worker remains in its pane until the owned daemon is stopped. Receipt paths
are local to this example's daemon host; this is not a remote-file API.

## Inspect a typed failure

This cancels a read before it acquires data, then handles `command-cancelled`
and returns the retained dispatch evidence:

<!-- example:condition -->
```lisp
(defun cancelled-read (client)
  "Demonstrate typed failure evidence using a read cancelled before acquisition."
  (let ((token (tm:make-cancellation-token)))
    (tm:cancel token)
    (handler-case
        (progn (tm:fetch-snapshot client :cancel-token token)
               (error "A cancelled read unexpectedly completed"))
      (tm:command-cancelled (condition)
        (let ((outcome (tm:error-outcome condition)))
          (list :condition (type-of condition)
                :status (and outcome (tm:outcome-status outcome))
                :phase (and outcome (tm:outcome-phase outcome))))))))
```
<!-- /example -->

```lisp
(tm:with-client (client :socket-path *socket-path*) (cancelled-read client))
```

This handler inspects evidence and returns; it never retries a command.
Post-dispatch cancellation of a mutation can have a different status or phase.
See the [condition reference](api.md#command-cancelled-type).

## Terminate the owned server

Closing a client leaves its daemon alive. This checked helper uses the separate
[`kill-server`](api.md#kill-server-function) operation only for the explicit
socket passed by the caller. It accepts success only after the operation proves
both dispatch and daemon exit:

<!-- example:termination -->
```lisp
(defun terminate-owned-server (socket-path &key (program "tmux"))
  "Terminate the explicitly selected owned server and return its proven outcome."
  (tm:with-client (client :program program :socket-path socket-path)
    (let ((outcome (tm:kill-server client)))
      (assert (eq :succeeded (tm:outcome-status outcome)))
      (assert (eq :server-terminated (tm:outcome-phase outcome)))
      outcome)))
```
<!-- /example -->

Run it only for the private tutorial endpoint:

```lisp
(terminate-owned-server *socket-path*)
```

## Clean up

Exit the REPL:

```lisp
(uiop:quit)
```

In the original shell, terminate only the daemon created for this tutorial:

```console
$ python3 tools/stop-example.py --already-terminated "$LIBTMUX_DEMO_DIR"
```

The helper proves the retained daemon PID exited, rejects a replaced socket,
then removes the owned witness, receipt and stale socket file. Tmux 3.3a can
leave its socket behind after exit. The automated runner executes the same Lisp
termination function before this file cleanup. If an earlier example fails, it
uses the retained witness to terminate and reap only this tutorial daemon.

# Captured objects

`fetch-snapshot` reads the selected daemon and returns a native CLOS graph.
Acquisition checks the [supported command-alias configuration](operations.md#command-aliases-and-daemon-configuration)
before listing state.
`sessions`, `windows`, `panes`, `window-links` and `clients` then return fresh
vectors from that observation. These getters, field access, printing,
`same-entity-p` and `entity-data` perform no tmux calls. Captured objects remain
usable after the client closes.

`fetch-sessions`, `fetch-windows`, `fetch-panes` and `fetch-clients` acquire a
complete graph and return the corresponding vector. Repeated fetches read
again. Retain one snapshot when several operations should inspect the same
observation. Filtering a retained vector will use ordinary sequence functions;
the separate [`libtmux/query`](queries.md) system also provides validated local
filters, relation quantifiers and eager QuerySets.

## Entities, links and order

A snapshot contains each physical session, window and pane once. A
`window-link` records a session, index and expected physical window. Linking a
window twice into one session creates two links; linking it elsewhere creates
another. Session-relative active-window state belongs to the link.

| Accessor | Captured result |
| --- | --- |
| `sessions snapshot` | Physical sessions in tmux's observed order |
| `windows snapshot`, `panes snapshot` | Physical entities in first-occurrence order |
| `window-links snapshot` | Every contextual link in listing order |
| `window-links session` | That session's links in observed index order |
| `windows session` | One window per link; repeated physical windows remain repeated |
| `panes window` | Physical panes in captured pane order |
| `window-links window` | Every link to that physical window |
| `window pane`, `window link` | The captured physical window |
| `session link`, `session attached-client` | The captured session |
| `clients snapshot`, `clients session` | Attached-client rows, preserving order and multiplicity |

An attached tmux client is an `attached-client` observation. It is distinct from
the library's connection `client`. Repeated target names are retained; a name
does not establish identity.

## Values and ownership

`field-value` returns value and presence as two values. Present false is
`nil, t`; an absent optional field is `nil, nil`. Empty names and pane titles
are present strings. Current command/path may be absent when tmux reports an
empty value. An empty or zero pane PID is absent, while the captured dead flag
retains the daemon version's reported meaning. Never infer one from the other.

The convenience readers `name`, `active-p`, `width`, `height`, `index`,
`current-command`, `current-path`, `title` and `dead-p` follow the same presence
contract. Paths remain text from tmux; they are not normalized as local paths.
Unknown fields and unloaded relations signal `field-unavailable`.

Every public mutable result is owned by the caller: strings, relation vectors,
provenance and projection containers are copied. Entity observations can be
shared between result vectors. Changing a returned vector or string does not
change the capture. Deliberate private-slot mutation is unsupported.

`entity-data` returns a finite plist with captured fields, provenance and
relationship identifiers. It omits absent optional fields and retains present
false values. It contains no operational handles or recursive object graph.
Use `id` to inspect identity: physical IDs are strings; link IDs are
`(session-id index expected-window-id)`; attached-client row IDs have meaning
only within that observation.

## Identity and refresh

`same-entity-p` compares model, connection context, generation and captured ID.
Two clients have distinct contexts even when connected to the same daemon.
Window-link identity retains its expected window and index; the index is a
mutable locator. Attached-client identity is scoped to one snapshot.

`refresh` takes the connection client and an existing entity or snapshot. It
acquires a replacement without changing the old observation. A different
server generation, missing target or changed link mapping signals
`stale-target`. Refreshing an attached client requires a unique live target
name and matching PID, creation time and tty presence; the returned object's
observation identity is new.

The native Linux witness includes daemon PID, daemon startup, socket inode and
device, kernel process-start identity and a retained pidfd. This distinguishes
server replacement even if tmux reuses its numeric IDs and startup second.
The daemon version and selected executable version are recorded separately.

Acquisition first verifies the selected endpoint, then pins subsequent commands
to its canonical path. Every listing carries a tagged witness produced on the
same server connection as its rows, including an empty listing. A changed peer
invalidates the attempt. Final continuity checks detect server replacement and
persistent selected-endpoint changes. This does not make graph acquisition
transactional: tmux state can change between the listing commands.

## Bounds and failures

Provenance records monotonic acquisition bounds and Common Lisp universal-time
bounds, as well as tmux's Unix server-start time. Duplicate physical rows must
agree. References, contextual pane order, counts and active states are checked.
Contradictory captures retry at most twice, then signal `incomplete-snapshot`.
Retries share the original deadline and byte budget.

The default total timeout is 30 seconds and total output cap is 16 MiB, inherited
from the client. Defaults also bound each listing to 100,000 rows, the graph to
100,000 entities, and each encoded field to 1 MiB. `:timeout`, `:output-limit`,
`:row-limit`, `:entity-limit`, `:field-limit` and `:cancel-token` configure these
limits on fetch operations. Decoding and graph construction check cancellation
and the same deadline as subprocess work.

A confirmed live daemon with zero sessions returns empty vectors. A missing
daemon or failed listing signals a condition; neither becomes an empty result.
Acquisition uses tmux's no-start option and never starts a daemon implicitly.
The current core observes entities reachable from sessions; it does not claim
an inventory of detached internal tmux objects outside that graph.

# Native queries

`libtmux/query` compiles inert keyword-headed data into a reusable Common Lisp
function over captured entities and their registered relationships. Compilation
and evaluation are local: they do not acquire, refresh or mutate tmux. Use an
ordinary Lisp function when a one-off selection does not need validation or
inspection.

[Query API](query-api.md) · [Captured fields](fields.md) ·
[Runnable tutorial](tutorial.md#select-and-project-locally)

## Load without global nicknames

Load the separate query system. It loads `libtmux` but no regex, JSON or thread
library:

```lisp
(asdf:load-system "libtmux/query")
```

Applications can choose package-local nicknames:

```lisp
(defpackage #:my-tmux-tool
  (:use #:cl)
  (:local-nicknames (#:tm #:libtmux)
                    (#:q #:libtmux.query)))

(in-package #:my-tmux-tool)
```

The library does not claim the short global package names `tm` or `q`.

## Compile once and match locally

Quoted lists are data. `compile-filter` validates the root model, operator,
field, arity and operand types; it never calls `eval`.

```lisp
(defparameter *editors*
  (q:compile-filter
   :pane
   '(:and
     (:= :pane/active t)
     (:in :pane/current-command ("nvim" "vim"))
     (:>= :pane/width 100))))
```

Use the returned genuine function with standard sequence operations:

```lisp
(remove-if (complement (q:predicate *editors*)) panes)
```

Or request a fresh simple vector with original order and multiplicity:

```lisp
(q:matching *editors* panes)
```

`matching` accepts a proper finite list or a non-string vector. It honors fill
pointers and displaced vectors, validates the complete outer container before
evaluation, and shares one execution budget across the traversal. It retains
the captured handles; it does not copy the object graph.

## Scalar semantics

| Form | Fields | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `(:= field value)` | Text, integer, Boolean | Typed equality |
| `(:< field n)`, `(:<= field n)`, `(:> field n)`, `(:>= field n)` | Integer | Mathematical integer comparison |
| `(:in field values)` | Text, integer, Boolean | Typed finite membership |
| `(:contains field text)` | Text | Case-sensitive substring search |
| `(:starts-with field text)` | Text | Case-sensitive prefix |
| `(:and ...)`, `(:or ...)`, `(:not expression)` | Expressions | Ordered Boolean composition |
| `(:present field)`, `(:missing field)` | Scalar | Captured presence |

Text uses content comparison. Integers are Common Lisp integers; wire-decoding
bounds do not truncate query operands. Ratios and floats are invalid. Empty AND
is true, empty OR and empty membership are false. A bare `nil` filter is
invalid.

Presence is separate from truth. `(:= :pane/active nil)` compares a present
false value. A scalar comparison on an absent optional field is false, so NOT
of that comparison is true. Use `:present` when absence must be excluded.
Missing required capture data signals `field-unavailable`.

## Add optional regex operators

Load CL-PPCRE support without changing the dependency boundary of core or
`libtmux/query`:

```lisp
(asdf:load-system "libtmux/regex")
```

The operand is owned declarative data: the engine, pattern and closed scanner
options. Search and full match are separate operations:

```lisp
(q:compile-filter
 :pane
 '(:regex-search :pane/current-command
   (:cl-ppcre "^(n?vim)$" :case-insensitive-mode t)))
```

Supported Boolean options are `:case-insensitive-mode`, `:multi-line-mode`,
`:single-line-mode` and `:extended-mode`. The scanner is compiled once. A match
at position zero is true. An absent optional text field is false. Query visit
limits do not interrupt CL-PPCRE scanner execution; use regex only with trusted
local patterns and inputs appropriate to that engine.

The separate [query interchange guide](query-interchange.md) shows bounded JSON
round trips and the explicit regex read opt-in.

## Traverse captured relationships

Relation forms compile their child expression for the registered target model:

| Form | Relation | Empty or missing behavior |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `(:any relation expression)` | To-many | False on an empty relation |
| `(:all relation expression)` | To-many | True on an empty relation |
| `(:none relation expression)` | To-many | True on an empty relation |
| `(:is relation expression)` | To-one | False when the target is absent |

This expression requires one pane to be both active and running `nvim`:

```lisp
(q:compile-filter
 :session
 '(:any :session/window-links
   (:is :link/window
    (:any :window/panes
     (:and (:= :pane/active t)
           (:= :pane/current-command "nvim"))))))
```

Two separate `:any` forms may match different panes. Missing or unloaded
relationship data signals `field-unavailable`; it is not treated as a known
empty collection. `required-relations` reports every traversed relation in
first-occurrence order.

## Keep eager local selections in a QuerySet

QuerySet is an optional collection convenience, not a replacement for Common
Lisp sequences. It owns a simple-vector container and remains eager:

```lisp
(let* ((all (q:from panes :model :pane))
       (editors (q:where all *editors*))
       (wide (q:where-if editors (lambda (pane) (>= (tm:width pane) 120))))
       (ordered (q:order-by wide #'> :key #'tm:width)))
  (q:items ordered))
```

`from`, `where`, `where-if` and `order-by` return new objects. `items` returns a
fresh simple vector. `order-by` uses `stable-sort` on a private copy, so equal
keys retain input order; its predicate and key follow Common Lisp's ordinary
sorting callback contract. `where-if` calls its native function once per item
in input order. A declared model is checked against every item; an empty
QuerySet can carry its model explicitly, while `where` can take the model from
its compiled filter. `one` and `one-or-none` accept QuerySets directly.

## Inspect owned query data

Inspection returns fresh ordinary data:

```lisp
(q:expression *editors*)
```

```lisp
(q:required-fields *editors*)
```

```lisp
(q:explain *editors*)
```

Changing the source form after compilation, or changing an inspection result,
does not alter the compiled filter. `fields` returns fresh registry metadata for
one of `:session`, `:window`, `:pane`, `:window-link` or `:client`. Here
`:client` means a captured attached tmux client, not the connection object.

## Select strictly before mutation

`one` requires exactly one item. `one-or-none` returns two values so an empty
selection differs from a singleton containing `nil`:

```lisp
(multiple-value-bind (pane present-p)
    (q:one-or-none (q:matching *editors* panes))
  (when present-p
    (tm:capture-pane client pane)))
```

Both functions validate the complete bounded input before returning a
candidate. Zero items signal `no-match` from `one`; multiple positions signal
`ambiguous-match`. Repeated references count as repeated positions. The
condition reports whether its count is exact and exposes a fresh bounded sample.
This ordering prevents a dependent mutation from running before uniqueness is
established.

## Resource limits and failures

The defaults bound nesting to 64 containers, compilation to 10,000 structure
visits, one membership to 1,000 values, one string to 65,536 characters,
retained query text to 1,048,576 characters, selection to 100,000 items and one
execution scope to 1,000,000 expression and relation visits. `compile-filter`,
`matching`, QuerySet constructors, `one` and `one-or-none` expose narrower
keyword limits for untrusted in-process data.

Cycles, dotted lists, invalid operators, wrong field types and unavailable
optional systems signal `invalid-filter`. Limit exhaustion signals its subtype
`query-limit-exceeded`. Applying a compiled filter to the wrong captured model
or to a plist signals `invalid-query-target`. Diagnostics retain bounded type
and path data; they do not print an unbounded caller object.

External configuration files need the later bounded JSON codec. Disabling
`*read-eval*` alone does not turn the Common Lisp reader into a query parser.

## Load only what the application uses

Enable the two regex operators:

```lisp
(asdf:load-system "libtmux/regex")
```

Enable versioned JSON reading and writing:

```lisp
(asdf:load-system "libtmux/json")
```

Load both before reading a document containing regex nodes. Neither system

## Compile a reusable regex

<!-- example:regex -->
```lisp
(defparameter *cat-command-filter*
  (q:compile-filter
   :pane
   '(:regex-full-match :pane/current-command
     (:cl-ppcre "CAT" :case-insensitive-mode t))))

(defun cat-pane-data (snapshot)
  "Return owned data for captured panes whose command is exactly cat; no I/O."
  (map 'vector #'tm:entity-data
       (q:matching *cat-command-filter* (tm:panes snapshot))))
```
<!-- /example -->

The compiled filter retains owned pattern/options data and one prepared
CL-PPCRE scanner. `:regex-search` accepts a match anywhere;
`:regex-full-match` requires the complete captured string. An absent field does
not match. Parser and query visit limits do not interrupt scanner execution.

## Round-trip a compiled filter

Applications can give `libtmux.json` a package-local nickname such as `j`.
Writing returns a fresh string by default:

<!-- example:filterdocument -->
```lisp
(defun round-trip-filter-document (snapshot)
  "Round-trip the checked regex filter and apply it to one retained snapshot."
  (let* ((document (j:write-filter *cat-command-filter*))
         (restored (j:read-filter document :allow-regex t)))
    (values document
            (map 'vector #'tm:entity-data
                 (q:matching restored (tm:panes snapshot))))))
```
<!-- /example -->

Without `:allow-regex t`, `read-filter` rejects a regex node before compiling
its scanner. Non-regex documents need only `libtmux/json`.

`write-filter` returns a fresh string unless given an open output character
stream. It does not open pathnames or close a caller-owned stream.

## Wire envelope

The native schema is `libtmux.lisp.filter/1`:

```json
{"schema":"libtmux.lisp.filter/1","model":"pane","registryVersion":1,"expression":["and",["=","pane/active",false],["in","pane/current-command",[]]]}
```

The root object is closed and requires exactly the named members. Duplicate or
unknown members, unknown models/operators/fields, wrong arities and unsupported
registry versions signal `invalid-filter-document`. External names remain
strings until allowlist lookup; the decoder never interns them.

Boolean false is JSON `false`. An empty membership is `[]`. JSON `null` is
distinct and rejected because registry version 1 has no nullable query operand.
Numeric operands are integers; decimal and exponent syntax is rejected before
Jzon converts the token.
Native closures and QuerySet callbacks are not serializable recipes.

This schema belongs to the Common Lisp port. Similar JSON from another port is
not compatible without operator-by-operator conformance evidence.

## Decoder limits

`read-filter` accepts one complete JSON string and defaults to:

| Limit | Default |
| --- | ---: |
| UTF-8 input | 1 MiB |
| Nesting depth | 64 |
| JSON nodes | 10,000 |
| One string | 65,536 characters |
| Membership operands | 1,000 |
| Decimal digits in one numeric token | 128 |

Override a limit with the corresponding keyword argument. An exhausted bound
signals `filter-document-limit-exceeded`; `document-limit` identifies the
bound and `document-path` returns an owned location vector. Jzon syntax failures
and native-query validation failures remain available through `error-cause`.

Named operations take the connection client first and a captured target where
needed. They read current state to validate the target, then use its identity.
Earlier captures remain unchanged. Every operation accepts `:cancel-token`,
`:timeout` and `:output-limit`; the latter two default to the client settings
and cover validation, dispatch and any follow-up acquisition together.

The current APIs require a live daemon. `new-session` creates a session there;
daemon bootstrap is a separate unfinished part of the implementation.

| `rename-window`, `rename-session` | Physical entity; command outcome with optional replacement |
| `select-window` | Window link, preserving session/index context |
| `select-pane` | Physical pane |
| `next-window`, `previous-window`, `last-window` | Session; outcome containing its selected window link |
| `last-pane` | Physical window; outcome containing its selected pane |

| `new-window` | Captured session; outcome containing the physical window |
| `split-pane` | Captured pane; outcome containing the new pane |
| `capture-pane` | Pane; UTF-8 text and diagnostic outcome as two values |
| `capture-pane-bytes` | Pane; owned octets and diagnostic outcome as two values |
| `send-text`, `send-keys`, `send-prefix` | Pane; command outcome for the send request |
| `respawn-pane`, `respawn-window` | Physical target; explicit process replacement and optional captured result |
| `pipe-pane` | Pane; explicit shell source, direction and daemon-owned pipe |
| `clear-history`, `copy-mode` | Pane; command outcome |
| `resize-pane`, `resize-window` | Physical target; outcome with optional replacement |
| `select-layout`, `next-layout`, `previous-layout` | Physical window; outcome with optional replacement |
| `link-window`, `move-window`, `break-pane` | Explicit link/session/index context; outcome containing the destination link |

`new-window :index` chooses a free session index. `split-pane` accepts
`:horizontal` (left/right) or `:vertical` (top/bottom), with a cell `:size` or
`:percent`. Creation returns a fresh captured entity through `outcome-value`.

## Names and child commands

Names and creation `:cwd` strings are literal. Rename's `:format-p t` explicitly
requests tmux format expansion. Tmux can normalize or reject a name; inspect the
replacement observation for the resulting name. Cwd text follows tmux's own
relative-path rules.

Creation accepts a nonempty `:command` list/vector of argv strings or a separate
`:shell-command` string. Omission selects tmux's default shell. Supplying an
empty argv is invalid. Strings may contain spaces, quotes, semicolons, dollar
signs, backslashes and Unicode; the encoder preserves their argument boundaries.
One-element argv starts that executable with no added program argument.
`:environment` is a list/vector of `(name . value)` string pairs.

The final encoded tmux command is limited to 16,000 UTF-8 bytes, including NUL
terminators between argv entries. Nested command quoting counts toward this
limit. Oversized named commands fail before their payload is dispatched. They
are never silently split into multiple mutations.

## Terminal input

`send-text` preserves literal text such as `C-c`; `:enter t` appends one Return
key in the same request. `send-keys` accepts a nonempty list/vector of tmux key
strings and a positive `:repeat` count. Tmux recognizes names such as `C-c` and
`Enter`, and falls back to literal input for unrecognized strings. `send-prefix`
uses the configured prefix; `:second t` selects prefix2.

The pane's current tmux mode handles input. Successful dispatch means tmux
processed the send request; it does not establish application consumption or
readiness. Coordinate dependent work through an application signal.

`copy-mode` enters copy mode; `:page-up t` scrolls on entry, and `:exit t` exits.
Page-up and exit are mutually exclusive. `clear-history` removes retained tmux
history; it does not promise to clear the application's current screen.

## Geometry and selection

`resize-pane` and `resize-window` accept positive cell `:width`/`:height`, or a
`:direction` (`:left`, `:right`, `:up`, `:down`) with positive `:amount` (default
one). Absolute dimensions range from 1 through 10,000, the common supported
range. Relative amounts range from 1 through 2,147,483,647. Tmux may clamp the
actual layout; the replacement observation contains the resulting dimensions.

Pane `:zoom t` toggles zoom. Window `:fit :smallest` or `:fit :largest` fits the
attached clients. These modes cannot be combined with dimensions or direction.
A window resize sets tmux's `window-size` option to manual.

`select-layout` accepts `:even-horizontal`, `:even-vertical`, `:main-horizontal`,
`:main-vertical`, `:tiled`, or `(:custom "tmux-layout-description")`.
Tmux validates custom checksums and geometry. Layout operations unzoom the
window. `next-layout` and `previous-layout` follow tmux's layout ordering.

`next-window`, `previous-window` and `last-window` take a captured session and
return its newly observed active **window link** through `outcome-value`.
Next and previous accept `:activity t` to restrict selection to alerting windows.
`last-pane` takes a physical window and returns its observed active pane.
Tmux signals when no last selection exists. These operations and geometry
accept `:observe nil` to omit follow-up acquisition.

## Links and pane placement

`link-window` and `move-window` take a source **window link**, a destination
session and an explicit free index. The source link preserves session group
context. Neither overwrites an occupied index. Moving removes only the selected
source link; removing a session's last link can destroy that session.
`unlink-window` refuses a last reference unless `:kill-if-last t` is explicit;
tmux session groups affect its last-reference check.

`swap-windows` takes two links and returns their replacement links in argument
order. `:select t` selects the affected indexes; omission retains current
indexes. An old link whose index now points at another window is stale.

`move-pane` and `join-pane` take source and destination physical panes.
`:direction`, `:size`, `:percent`, `:before` and `:full-size` control placement;
`:detached t` is the default. An emptied source window and all its links are
destroyed. With `:detached nil`, tmux chooses the session context of the physical
destination. Percentage sizing follows the installed tmux semantics: with
`:full-size t`, 3.3a uses the destination pane's dimensions while 3.8 uses the
whole window. Use `:size` for cell-based control.

`break-pane` takes the pane, its explicit source link, a destination session
and a free index. This source link matters when the pane is its window's only
pane: tmux moves that link while preserving other links and the physical window.
The outcome contains the destination link. Its optional `:name` is literal.

`swap-panes` preserves physical IDs and returns replacements in argument order.
`rotate-window` moves pane positions `:up` (default) or `:down` and advances
the active pane. Both accept `:preserve-zoom t`. Placement operations preserve
older observations; a successful operation may have a separate observation
failure. Unlink has no replacement to observe.

## Pane processes

`respawn-pane` restarts its process. `respawn-window` restarts the physical
window as one pane, retaining its first pane and destroying every other pane,
including through other session links. Neither kills a running process unless
`:kill t` is supplied. Omit both `:command` and `:shell-command` to reuse the
stored command; explicit argv, shell text, cwd and environment follow creation.
By default, `outcome-value` supplies a new observation. Earlier captures remain
local and unchanged. A fast-exiting process can disappear before acquisition.

`pipe-pane` accepts explicit `:shell-command` source. It preserves literal `#`
and `%` text by default; `:format-p t` enables tmux format and time expansion
before the shell runs. Literal commands must fit tmux's 8,191-byte time-format
capacity after format escaping. `:direction` is `:output` (pane to shell),
`:input` (shell to pane) or `:both`. Omitting the command closes the pipe.
`:toggle t` closes an existing pipe without starting its replacement.

Pipe success acknowledges configuration. It does not prove shell startup,
command success or data consumption. Coordinate dependent work through an
application signal. Tmux owns the pipe child, and closing the library client
leaves it running. Pipe replacement or explicit closure releases the pane's
connection to that child.

## Buffers

`list-buffers` returns a fresh vector of plists with `:buffer/name`, `:buffer/size`
in bytes and `:buffer/created` in Unix seconds. It preserves tmux's listing
order, limits decoding to 10,000 rows by default, and returns `#()` when empty.
Names are mutable locators, not captured entity identities.

`set-buffer` accepts a literal NUL-free string or an octet vector. Octets travel
through tmux's stdin buffer loader and preserve NUL and invalid UTF-8. `:append t`
is supported for strings. `show-buffer` returns owned octets without decoding.
Both accept a literal `:name`; setting without a name creates an automatic buffer.
Creation through set/load rejects backslashes, ASCII controls and DEL before
I/O because tmux versions otherwise rewrite or reject them. Spaces and Unicode
are supported. Looking up an existing buffer preserves its actual name.

`show-buffer` uses one ordinary unattached tmux client with stdout reserved for
buffer bytes. The same live server guard, operation budget and alias audit apply.
It succeeds only after normal process completion and complete pipe draining,
with exit zero and empty stderr. A hook cannot hide an error by changing its
exit status. Post-launch read failure retains partial output and diagnostics;
it does not prove that the read was never dispatched. Buffer contents are never
parsed as receipts or errors. This contract does not apply to control mode.

`load-buffer` and `save-buffer` take literal file-path strings; `:name` selects
the buffer. Save overwrites unless `:append t` is supplied. Relative paths follow
the tmux command client's cwd. A literal file named `-` must be spelled `./-`;
use set/show for in-memory bytes. Empty input or an empty loaded file is tmux's
no-op and preserves any existing buffer.
Save success records tmux's reported completion; it does not independently
verify file contents or durability. Tmux 3.3a can suppress some file-write errors.

`paste-buffer` takes a physical pane and optional `:name`. Newlines become Return
by default. `:raw t` preserves them; a separate `:separator` string replaces
each newline. `:bracketed t` requests bracket markers when the pane enabled
bracketed paste. `:verbatim t` preserves all bytes, disables newer tmux control-byte
sanitization, and cannot add separators or bracket markers. It chooses flags
from the live daemon version. `:delete t` removes the selected buffer after pasting. Input
disablement and application consumption remain tmux/application concerns.

`delete-buffer :name` requires tmux 3.4 or newer. On 3.3a it signals
`unsupported-capability` before dispatch, because that release can delete an
unrelated top buffer when a named buffer is missing. The condition exposes
`error-feature`, `error-required-version` and `error-actual-version`; the check
uses the live daemon's version, independently of the selected executable.

Omitting a buffer name for show, save, paste or delete uses tmux's default:
the newest buffer on 3.3a, and the newest **automatic** buffer from 3.4 onward.
It does not select the newest explicitly named buffer on modern tmux.

## Configuration mutations

[`set-option`](api.md#set-option-function) and
[`unset-option`](api.md#unset-option-function) address one explicit tmux option
table. Server and global scopes reject a target. Session, window and pane
scopes require a captured target of that type, so the normal generation and
last-moment target guards apply. The exact live daemon version selects the
reviewed option catalog after preflight; the executable's version cannot
silently substitute for it. The current catalogs cover the twelve exact
supported releases from 3.3a through 3.8. An unreviewed neighboring release
signals an error; see [capabilities and current limits](capabilities.md).

Literal writes validate the catalog's native Boolean, integer, choice and text
type before payload dispatch. `nil` is a valid false option value and becomes
tmux `off`. `:format-p t` instead accepts explicit tmux format text and lets the
daemon validate its expanded value. Registered array elements use `:key` and
never allocate a vector by the greatest numeric key. Without `:key`, an array
value uses the option's native tmux list grammar and may create several entries;
use `:key` when the value must remain one literal entry. `:append t` is accepted
only where tmux implements it: strings, keyed string-array values and unkeyed
array assignment. Public user-option writes accept the reversible
`@[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+` name grammar.

[`set-hook`](api.md#set-hook-function) accepts explicit tmux command source; it
does not parse the source as Lisp or execute it locally. Ordinary installation
never uses tmux's immediate-run flag. Tmux can still run a registered native
after-hook such as `after-set-hook` as a consequence of processing the command.
Keyed hook entries do not support appending command text; unkeyed append adds
hook entries through tmux's array grammar. Use
[`unset-hook`](api.md#unset-hook-function) to remove the hook. Registered hooks
stay separate from ordinary option writes, and the live catalog gates dynamic
event sources.

[`set-environment`](api.md#set-environment-function) writes one raw global or
captured-session environment table. It accepts literal text by default,
explicit format expansion through `:format-p t`, and tmux's hidden flag.
[`unset-environment`](api.md#unset-environment-function) deletes an entry;
[`remove-environment`](api.md#remove-environment-function) stores tmux's
removal marker. A tombstone, absence and a present empty string remain distinct.
Names use `[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*` so later named acquisition is reversible.

All seven operations return a
[`command-outcome`](api.md#command-outcome-type), retain effective arguments
and diagnostics, and never retry uncertain mutations. Decoded configuration
readers remain under development; use [`run-command`](api.md#run-command-function)
only when raw tmux argv and its weaker target contract are intentional.

## Explicit termination

[`kill-pane`](api.md#kill-pane-function),
[`kill-window`](api.md#kill-window-function) and
[`kill-session`](api.md#kill-session-function) accept one captured physical
target. The same preflight and last-moment guards used by other named mutations
reject a missing, replaced or foreign-generation target. These functions do not
expose tmux's broad `-a` forms. Killing a physical window removes all its links;
killing a session removes that session's links and any now-unreferenced panes.

[`kill-server`](api.md#kill-server-function) is deliberately separate from
[`close-client`](api.md#close-client-function). Closing releases library-owned
resources and leaves tmux alive. Server termination succeeds only after a
pre-dispatch receipt and readiness of the pidfd retained for the daemon accepted
during this call's preflight prove both dispatch and process exit. Daemon death
without the receipt remains `:unknown` because another actor could have
terminated it. After observed death, the client remains open but its generation
is invalidated; retained captures still support local traversal and projection.

All four operations are destructive and never retry automatically. Select the
target once, establish cardinality before dispatch, and inspect a retained
condition outcome when completion is uncertain.

## Outcomes and target checks

Mutators return `command-outcome`. `outcome-value` returns a value and presence
as two values. Rename and selection accept `:observe nil` to omit follow-up
acquisition. Otherwise a successful mutation followed by failed acquisition
still has status `:succeeded`, no value, and an `outcome-observation-error`.

| Evidence | Outcome |
| --- | --- |
| Preflight failed or live guard explicitly rejected the target | `:not-dispatched` |
| Completion receipt, successful tmux process exit and empty stderr | `:succeeded` |
| Completion receipt and nonzero process exit | `:failed` |
| Successful process exit with diagnostic output | `:unknown` |
| Dispatched operation lacks required receipts, or transport lost completion | `:unknown` |
| Server pidfd proves exit but the pre-dispatch receipt is missing | `:unknown` |
| Server receipt and retained pidfd both prove explicit termination | `:succeeded`, phase `:server-terminated` |
| Server exit wait fails after dispatch | `:unknown`, reason `:server-exit-unobserved`; cause retained |

The outcome retains exit status, diagnostic bytes, effective arguments and
elapsed time. A failed command queue can have completed effects; it does not
imply rollback. An unknown mutation is never automatically retried.

Validation checks the live server generation and captured entity identity.
The dispatch connection checks the daemon again and checks physical targets or
session/index/window mappings immediately before the payload. A reused link
index signals `stale-target`. These checks do not make selection and mutation
a transaction; tmux hooks and other clients can change state.

Capture preserves whitespace and trailing lines. The text API strictly decodes
UTF-8; decoding failures retain the client and raw command outcome. The byte API
copies output without decoding. Its flags expose tmux's history, wrapping,
alternate-screen, pending-output and escape modes; they do not reconstruct
terminal bytes that tmux did not retain.

## Command aliases and daemon configuration

Named APIs require the original built-in command meanings and stable
`command-alias` configuration during each call. `show-options` is the trusted
bootstrap spelling used to inspect aliases. It must remain the built-in command.
The audit cannot safely inspect an arbitrary override of itself or prevent
configuration changes after inspection.

Before acquisition or a named operation, the library reads `command-alias` and
signals `unsupported-configuration` for collisions with reserved command names.
`error-setting` identifies the option; `error-commands` returns the colliding
spellings. The reserved list is maintained in
[command-policy.lisp](../src/command-policy.lisp). Other alias names are allowed.
The check conservatively rejects an apparent reserved assignment on any line
of a multiline alias value.

Configured tmux hooks keep their ordinary behavior. The library does not remove
aliases or hooks from the user's daemon. `run-command` remains an explicit raw
escape hatch with tmux's command grammar and no captured-target or alias audit.

# Clients and subprocess commands

`open-client` checks the selected tmux executable and returns a connection
scope. It does not start a daemon. Choose one of `:socket-name` or
`:socket-path`; omitting both selects tmux's default endpoint. `:config-file`
is passed explicitly when provided. Configuration strings are copied.

`with-client` closes the original client on every exit. The body supports
declarations and preserves multiple values. Rebinding its visible variable
does not change the resource to close. Closing releases the client's processes
and streams; it leaves the tmux daemon running.

## Command results

`run-command` takes a client and a finite list or vector of argv strings.
Supply `:effect :read` or `:effect :mutation` explicitly. Arguments bypass
shell parsing, but tmux's command and format grammar still applies. This
escape hatch does not validate captured target identities. Named entity
operations provide that validation; see the [operation contracts](operations.md).

The optional `:input` is an octet vector, copied before dispatch. Standard
output and diagnostic output are retained as bytes, including invalid UTF-8.
`outcome-stdout`, `outcome-stderr` and `outcome-arguments` return owned copies.
An external command failure signals a condition whose `error-outcome` retains
the result and whose `error-cause` retains an underlying failure when present.
`error-client` identifies the client, including a partially opened client that
still owns cleanup work. Retry `close-client` on that object if cleanup failed.

| Outcome status | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `:succeeded` | The child exited successfully and transport cleanup completed |
| `:failed` | The child reported a nonzero exit status |
| `:unknown` | Dispatch was possible but interruption, limits or cleanup prevented a complete result |
| `:not-dispatched` | Dispatch was prevented or the launcher positively reported an exec failure |

Raw `outcome-phase` records `:prepared`, `:launching`, `:dispatched` or
`:exited`; named operations also use `:preflight` and `:guard-rejected`.
Their [receipt and outcome policy](operations.md#outcomes-and-target-checks)
requires more evidence than the raw process runner. Inspect `outcome-reason`,
`outcome-exit-code` and retained diagnostics
as well. A command reporting failure can already have changed tmux; these
statuses do not promise rollback. The library never retries an uncertain
mutation automatically.

## Bounds and concurrency

The default command timeout is 30 seconds. The default combined stdout/stderr
limit is 16 MiB. Override these through client defaults or per-command
`:timeout` and `:output-limit`. The deadline includes launch and pipe service
after argument validation. A byte limit retains at most the configured count.
Input is written while both output pipes are drained, avoiding pipe deadlock.

One external operation owns a client at a time; concurrent work signals
`client-busy` before dispatch. Use separate clients for independent operations.
`make-cancellation-token` creates reusable one-way cancellation state; pass it
as `:cancel-token`, then call `cancel` from another thread. `cancel` returns
true only for the first request. An idle token owns no OS descriptors.
Cancellation signals `command-cancelled` from the operation and retains its
dispatch evidence; it does not undo a completed mutation.

Closing rejects new operations, requests cancellation and waits for the owner.
Normal process stop allows 50 ms before KILL and bounds teardown at 500 ms;
client close waits up to 750 ms for an active owner. A failed join signals
`cleanup-failed` and leaves the client closing. If child authority or cleanup
cannot be completed, the client retains the resources. Correct the underlying
resource problem and retry `close-client`. `client-cleanup-failures` returns a
fresh vector of retained secondary conditions.

Cleanup failure after a normal scope return signals. During an existing error
or nonlocal exit it is recorded without replacing that exit. Captured data
remains usable locally after client closure.

## Supported process boundary

The first backend targets SBCL on Linux x86-64. It requires pidfds, eventfd,
pidfd process-group signalling (Linux 6.9 or newer), their libc wrappers, and
Bash. Runtime checks reject missing capabilities. A private FIFO exec barrier
establishes process-group ownership before dispatch. It passes argv as separate
positional arguments and does not evaluate caller strings as shell source.
Only trusted native ELF target executables are accepted.

The backend forces `LC_ALL=C.UTF-8`, clears `TMUX` and `TMUX_PANE`, and normalizes
Bash startup variables used by its fixed launcher. It is not a byte-for-byte
environment transfer API. Use explicit tmux environment operations when those
are available. The private descriptor poll does not run application REPL
handlers. The library does not install a process-wide subreaper.

The bounds cover the supervised process group. They cannot force an
uninterruptible kernel syscall to return or contain a descendant that
deliberately leaves that group. An unfinished launch remains owned and is
reported as incomplete cleanup.

# Capabilities and current limits

The implemented systems suit bounded, blocking SBCL/Linux tmux automation with
captured graph traversal, native queries, explicit commands and declarative
workspace bootstrap. Persistent control/events remain future work.

| Area | Available now | Remaining work |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Runtime | SBCL 2.6.10, ASDF/UIOP 3.3.7, Linux x86-64, kernel 6.9+, Bash | Other implementation/OS support |
| Acquisition | Finite CLOS snapshots, explicit window links, identity, bounds and replacement observations | Complete all-version acceptance after further operations |
| Local processing | Ordinary lists/vectors, functions, owned plists, presence via multiple values, validated relation/regex queries and eager QuerySets | Source-side filter lowering |
| Operations | Creation, rename, selection, geometry, placement, input, buffers, respawn, shell pipes, typed option/hook/environment mutations, explicit entity/server termination | Decoded configuration readers, daemon bootstrap and attached-client operations |
| Concurrency | Synchronous calls; cancellation; one operation per client | Public asynchronous API and persistent control transport |
| Streaming/events | Complete bounded captures and byte buffers; daemon-owned `pipe-pane` | Native event/output subscriptions, bounded delivery, loss and backpressure |
| Workspace | Separate bounded JSON/native system, pure plans, explicit apply, no-op reuse and explicit-endpoint CLI | Deletion, process supervision and richer convergence are intentionally absent from v1 |
| MCP | Intentionally excluded by project policy | Use a separately maintained external integration if one becomes suitable |
| Optional integrations | Separate CL-PPCRE regex, bounded query JSON and workspace/CLI systems | Control ASDF system |
| Performance | No benchmark claims | Reproducible acquisition/filter/stream workloads and latency/allocation results |

The process backend services stdin/stdout/stderr through nonblocking descriptors
and a private poll loop. Public operations still block their caller. The library
has no Python `asyncio` API or event-loop integration; applying an asyncio
correctness rating to this native Common Lisp core would be misleading.
Independent clients can perform independent operations, but their identity
contexts differ. Do not pass one client's observations to another for mutation.

Portable Common Lisp plus ASDF/UIOP is the default dependency boundary. The
workspace consumer is a separate `libtmux/workspace` ASDF system over core and
the locked Jzon parser; its CLI is another separate system. External libraries
stay isolated in the optional systems that justify them.

MCP is intentionally outside this port's product scope; it is not an unfinished
package or release gate. An agent can still read the [public API](api.md),
[query API](query-api.md), [field registry](fields.md) and [tutorial](tutorial.md),
but these documents are not a protocol server. No terminal output stream or
lossless event-replay guarantee is implied by `pipe-pane`.

## Evidence and adoption

`mise run examples` executes the shipped Lisp examples on an owned socket with
empty tmux configuration. `mise run check` checks unit semantics, exported
docstrings, generated API/field/module pages, executable excerpts and local
documentation links. `mise run package` checks an isolated ASDF consumer;
`mise run integration` exercises the native transport and named operations.
See [verification](../verification.md) for evidence boundaries and commands.

Every-push CI checks exact tmux 3.3a and 3.8. A twelve-version workflow exists;
its configuration alone is not proof that all cells pass. The library rejects
plain 3.3. Runtime flags and some operation semantics depend on the live daemon
version as documented in the [operation contracts](operations.md).
Configuration mutations require one of the twelve exact reviewed catalogs from
3.3a through 3.8; an unreviewed neighboring release is rejected rather than
silently borrowing another version's schema.

A build-versus-adopt decision should check the platform boundary, required
operations, identity policy, synchronous concurrency model, diagnostics and
cleanup behavior against the actual application. Teams requiring subscriptions,
streaming or an MCP endpoint need a separate integration. The single maintainer
and unreleased status do not change those technical boundaries.

Benchmark evidence must report workload, graph size, tmux/toolchain versions,
acquisition counts, warm/cold timing, distributions and allocations. Test-loop
timings measure verification cost; they are not throughput benchmarks.
